terms: Battle of Little Bighorn 1876
The defeat of Custer's force by Sioux and Cheyenne warriors, a famous Native victory that nonetheless provoked harsher US reprisals.
California Gold Rush 1849
The mass migration of fortune-seekers to California after the discovery of gold, accelerating western settlement and statehood.
Manifest Destiny
The 19th-century belief that white Americans were destined to expand across the continent, justifying westward settlement and displacement of Native peoples.
Plains Indians
Native nations such as the Sioux who relied on the buffalo and clashed with settlers and the US army over land and survival.
The Oregon Trail
The long overland route west used by thousands of migrant families seeking land and opportunity in the 1840s and 1850s.
Transcontinental Railroad 1869
The rail link joining east and west coasts, transforming travel and trade and hastening the settlement of the West.

britain-health-the-people-c1000-to-prese.d: Britain: Health & the People c1000 to Present Day
terms: 1848 Public Health Act
First national public health legislation creating General Board of Health; permissive not compulsory, limited impact.
1875 Public Health Act
Compulsory Act forcing councils to provide clean water, drainage and sewers; passed under Disraeli's government.
Edwin Chadwick 1842
Reformer whose Report on the Sanitary Condition linked poverty, disease and slum housing, prompting 1848 Public Health Act.
Great Stink 1858
Hot summer when Thames sewage caused parliament to recess; led to Bazalgette's London sewer system.
Liberal Reforms 1906-11
Welfare measures including school meals, old age pensions (1908) and National Insurance Act (1911) under Asquith.
NHS 1948
National Health Service founded by Aneurin Bevan providing free healthcare at point of use, funded by taxation.
Berlin Wall 1961
Built by GDR on 13 August to stop East Germans fleeing; symbol of Iron Curtain until fall on 9 November 1989.
Brezhnev Doctrine
1968 Soviet policy justifying intervention to defend socialism in any Warsaw Pact country threatened by reform.
Hungarian Uprising 1956
Revolt led by Imre Nagy against Soviet control; crushed in November when Khrushchev sent 200,000 troops and tanks.
Korean War 1950-53
Conflict between communist North (Kim Il-sung) and US-backed South; UN forces under MacArthur; ended at 38th parallel.
Prague Spring 1968
Dubcek's reforms in Czechoslovakia ('socialism with a human face') crushed by Warsaw Pact invasion in August.
Soviet-Afghan War 1979-89
USSR's invasion to support communist regime; defeated by US-armed Mujahideen, weakening Soviet economy and morale.
Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin's attempt to force the Western powers out of Berlin by cutting land routes, defeated by the Allied airlift of supplies.
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
The tense standoff over Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba that brought the superpowers to the brink of war before a negotiated withdrawal.
Hungarian Uprising 1956
A revolt against Soviet control in Hungary, crushed by the Red Army, showing the limits of Western willingness to challenge the Eastern Bloc.
Prague Spring 1968
Reforms in Czechoslovakia seeking 'socialism with a human face', suppressed by a Warsaw Pact invasion reasserting Soviet dominance.
The Berlin Wall 1961
The barrier built by East Germany to stop its citizens fleeing to the West, becoming a stark symbol of the divided Cold War world.
Yalta and Potsdam 1945
Wartime conferences where the Allied leaders agreed on post-war Europe but exposed growing tensions between the USA and USSR.
Francis Drake
Privateer who circumnavigated globe 1577-80 and raided Spanish ports; vice-admiral against the Armada.
Globe Theatre 1599
Open-air playhouse built by Shakespeare's company in Southwark; held up to 3,000 spectators.
Mary Queen of Scots
Catholic claimant imprisoned 1568-87; executed after Babington Plot exposed Catholic conspiracy against Elizabeth.
Poor Laws 1601
System distinguishing 'deserving' from 'idle' poor; parishes raised rates to provide work or relief.
Religious Settlement 1559
Compromise establishing Protestant Church of England with Elizabeth as Supreme Governor; Act of Uniformity required attendance.
Spanish Armada 1588
Philip II's invasion fleet of 130 ships defeated by English ships and storms; symbolic Protestant victory.
Hyperinflation 1923
Catastrophic currency collapse during Ruhr crisis; bread reached 200 billion marks. Eroded middle-class trust in democracy.
Munich Putsch 1923
Hitler's failed coup in Bavaria; led to brief imprisonment where he wrote Mein Kampf, gave him national platform.
Night of the Long Knives 1934
30 June purge of SA leadership; Rohm and around 200 others murdered, consolidating Hitler's army support.
Reichstag Fire 1933
Fire blamed on Dutch communist van der Lubbe; used by Hitler as pretext for Enabling Act and one-party state.
Stresemann era 1924-29
Period of stability under chancellor Stresemann: Dawes Plan, Locarno Treaties, Weimar 'Golden Age'.
Treaty of Versailles 1919
Peace treaty imposing reparations, territorial losses and Article 231 (war guilt) on Germany after WWI.
Battle of Hastings 1066
Decisive battle on 14 October 1066 where William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson, killed by an arrow according to the Bayeux Tapestry.
Domesday Book 1086
Comprehensive land survey ordered by William I recording landholders, livestock and value for taxation across England.
Feudal System
Hierarchical land-holding pyramid: king grants land to barons for knight service; peasants worked land for protection.
Forest Laws
Harsh Norman laws reserving woodlands for royal hunting; punishments included blinding for poaching deer.
Harrying of the North 1069-70
William's brutal campaign destroying villages and crops in Yorkshire and Durham after rebellion; caused mass famine.
Motte and Bailey
Early Norman wooden castle design: raised mound (motte) with keep, enclosed courtyard (bailey) below for garrison.

power-the-people-c1170-to-present-day.d: Power & the People c1170 to Present Day
terms: Bill of Rights 1689
Constitutional law after Glorious Revolution limiting monarchy and establishing parliamentary sovereignty.
Chartists 1838-48
Working class movement demanding six points including universal male suffrage and secret ballot; three petitions failed.
English Civil War 1642-51
War between Charles I (Royalists) and Parliament (Roundheads); ended with Charles's execution in January 1649.
Magna Carta 1215
Charter limiting King John's power; clause 39 established no free man should be imprisoned except by lawful judgment.
Peterloo Massacre 1819
Cavalry charge into crowd of 60,000 demanding parliamentary reform at St Peter's Field, Manchester; 18 killed.
Simon de Montfort 1265
Baron who summoned first parliament including commoners (knights and burgesses) after defeating Henry III at Lewes.
Causes of the First World War
The long-term tensions of nationalism, imperialism, militarism and alliances that, with the 1914 assassination, plunged Europe into war.
Revolutions of 1848
A wave of liberal and nationalist uprisings across Europe demanding reform and unity, most of which were ultimately suppressed.
Scramble for Africa
The rapid late-19th-century partition of Africa among European powers, intensifying imperial rivalry and tension.
The Alliance System
The network of European treaties dividing the great powers into opposing blocs, increasing the danger of a general war.
Unification of Germany 1871
The creation of a German Empire under Prussian leadership, engineered by Bismarck through war and diplomacy.
Unification of Italy 1861
The drawing together of Italian states into a single kingdom, achieved by figures such as Cavour and Garibaldi.
Collapse of Communism 1989
The fall of the Berlin Wall and the unravelling of Soviet control in Eastern Europe, marking the end of the Cold War.
Rise of Hitler
The growth of Nazi power exploiting economic crisis and Versailles resentment, leading to Hitler becoming German Chancellor in 1933.
The Cold War
The post-1945 rivalry between the capitalist USA and communist USSR, dividing the world without direct war between the superpowers.
The League of Nations
The international body set up in 1920 to keep peace, weakened by US absence and its inability to stop aggression in the 1930s.
The Second World War 1939-45
The global conflict triggered by Nazi expansion, ending with Allied victory and reshaping the political order of the world.
Treaty of Versailles 1919
The peace settlement punishing Germany after the First World War with territorial losses, reparations and a war-guilt clause.
Hyperinflation 1923
Catastrophic currency collapse during Ruhr crisis; bread reached 200 billion marks. Eroded middle-class trust in democracy.
Munich Putsch 1923
Hitler's failed coup in Bavaria; led to brief imprisonment where he wrote Mein Kampf, gave him national platform.
Night of the Long Knives 1934
30 June purge of SA leadership; Rohm and around 200 others murdered, consolidating Hitler's army support.
Reichstag Fire 1933
Fire blamed on Dutch communist van der Lubbe; used by Hitler as pretext for Enabling Act and one-party state.
Stresemann era 1924-29
Period of stability under chancellor Stresemann: Dawes Plan, Locarno Treaties, Weimar 'Golden Age'.
Treaty of Versailles 1919
Peace treaty imposing reparations, territorial losses and Article 231 (war guilt) on Germany after WWI.
1905 Revolution
Uprising triggered by Bloody Sunday massacre; forced Tsar Nicholas II to issue October Manifesto promising Duma.
February Revolution 1917
Strikes and mutinies in Petrograd forced Nicholas II to abdicate; Provisional Government took power.
Five-Year Plans
Stalin's industrialisation programme from 1928; rapid heavy industry growth at huge human cost in gulags.
NEP 1921
New Economic Policy under Lenin allowing small private trade and ending grain requisitioning; restored agricultural output.
October Revolution 1917
Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd led by Lenin and Trotsky; stormed Winter Palace, overthrew Provisional Government.
War Communism
1918-21 policy nationalising industry and forcibly requisitioning grain to win Civil War; caused mass famine.
Great Depression
The severe economic slump after 1929: by 1933 around a quarter of the workforce was unemployed and shanty towns nicknamed 'Hoovervilles' spread.
Mass production
Assembly-line manufacturing pioneered by Henry Ford with the Model T, cutting costs so ordinary families could afford cars and consumer goods.
New Deal
Franklin D. Roosevelt's programme of relief, recovery and reform from 1933, using 'alphabet agencies' such as the CCC and TVA to fight the Depression.
Prohibition
The ban on making and selling alcohol under the 18th Amendment from 1920, which fuelled speakeasies, bootlegging and organised crime until repeal in 1933.
Roaring Twenties
The 1920s economic boom driven by mass production, consumer goods, advertising and credit, although farmers, Black Americans and older industries largely missed out.
Wall Street Crash 1929
The collapse of share prices in October 1929 that wiped out investors, triggered bank failures and helped tip the USA into the Great Depression.

changing-relations-northern-ireland-its-.d: Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1965-98
terms: Anglo-Irish Agreement 1985
Deal signed by Thatcher and FitzGerald giving the Republic of Ireland a consultative role in Northern Ireland affairs, provoking mass unionist protest under the slogan 'Ulster Says No'.
Bloody Sunday 1972
On 30 January 1972 British paratroopers shot dead thirteen civil rights marchers in Derry/Londonderry; Stormont was suspended and direct rule from London followed.
Civil Rights Movement
From 1967 NICRA campaigned against discrimination in housing allocation, jobs and local government voting; marches from 1968 met violence and escalated tensions.
Good Friday Agreement 1998
April 1998 settlement creating a power-sharing Assembly, North-South bodies and the principle of consent, endorsed by referendums on both sides of the border.
Terence O'Neill
Northern Ireland Prime Minister 1963-69 who pursued modernisation and met Irish Taoiseach Seán Lemass in 1965, but his cautious reforms angered hard-line unionists while disappointing nationalists.
The Troubles
Roughly thirty years of conflict from the late 1960s involving republican and loyalist paramilitaries and the security forces, killing around 3,500 people.
9/11 and the War on Terror
The 2001 al-Qaeda attacks on the USA led to wars in Afghanistan from 2001 and Iraq in 2003, reshaping international relations after the Cold War.
Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin cut road and rail routes into West Berlin; the Western Allies supplied the city by airlift for almost a year until he backed down.
Collapse of communism 1989-91
Gorbachev's reforms and revolutions across Eastern Europe, including the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, ended the Cold War as the USSR dissolved in 1991.
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
Thirteen-day standoff after the USA discovered Soviet missile sites on Cuba, ending when Khrushchev withdrew the missiles in return for American concessions.
Truman Doctrine 1947
America's pledge to support free peoples resisting communism, beginning with aid to Greece and Turkey and committing the USA to containment.
Yalta and Potsdam 1945
Allied conferences that agreed the division of Germany and Berlin into occupation zones, but exposed growing distrust between the USA and USSR.
Gestapo and SS
The secret state police and SS enforced conformity through surveillance, informers, arbitrary arrest and the concentration camp system.
Gleichschaltung
The Nazi 'coordination' of German society from 1933, bringing political parties, trade unions, media and culture under party control.
Hitler Youth
Nazi youth movements indoctrinating boys for military service and girls (League of German Maidens) for motherhood; membership was made effectively compulsory by 1939.
Persecution of the Jews
Escalating persecution from boycotts in 1933 through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and Kristallnacht in 1938 to the wartime Holocaust.
Propaganda
Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled press, film and radio, using rallies, cheap radio sets and spectacles like the 1936 Berlin Olympics to glorify the regime.
Women in Nazi Germany
Policy pushed women towards 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche' — children, kitchen, church — with marriage loans and the Mother's Cross rewarding large families.

peace-war-neutrality-britain-northern-ir.d: Peace, War & Neutrality: Britain, Northern Ireland & Ireland in WWII
terms: Battle of the Atlantic bases
Ports and airfields, especially around Derry/Londonderry, protected Atlantic convoys; American troops began arriving in Northern Ireland in 1942.
Belfast Blitz 1941
Luftwaffe raids on Belfast in April and May 1941 killed around a thousand people; the city was poorly defended and Dublin sent fire engines to help.
Conscription question
Conscription was never extended to Northern Ireland, largely because of expected nationalist opposition, so its forces were volunteers.
Irish neutrality (The Emergency)
Éire under de Valera stayed neutral throughout 1939-45, a period officially called 'the Emergency', asserting independence from Britain in foreign policy.
Northern Ireland's war effort
Harland & Wolff built ships, Short Brothers built aircraft, and farms supplied food, making Northern Ireland strategically valuable to Britain.
Treaty Ports
Naval bases at Berehaven, Cobh and Lough Swilly returned by Britain to Éire in 1938, denying the Royal Navy Atlantic bases once war began.
February Revolution 1917
Bread riots and strikes in Petrograd, joined by mutinying soldiers, forced Nicholas II to abdicate and ended Romanov rule.
Five-Year Plans
Stalin's drive from 1928 to industrialise the USSR rapidly, setting ambitious targets for coal, iron, steel and electricity.
Impact of the First World War
Military defeats, food shortages and inflation by 1917 destroyed faith in Tsar Nicholas II, who had taken personal command of the army in 1915.
New Economic Policy 1921
Lenin's tactical retreat that allowed peasants to sell surplus grain and permitted small private trade to revive the shattered economy.
October Revolution 1917
Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government in Petrograd, promising 'Peace, Bread and Land'.
War Communism
Harsh Civil War policy of grain requisitioning and nationalised industry that provoked peasant revolts and contributed to the famine of 1921.
Hoover's response
President Hoover stressed 'rugged individualism' and voluntary action, and though he later set up the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in 1932, he opposed direct federal relief.
Isolationism
After the First World War the USA refused to join the League of Nations and turned inwards, raising tariffs and restricting immigration with quota laws.
Opposition to the New Deal
Critics attacked from both sides: the Supreme Court struck down the NRA and AAA, while figures like Huey Long said reform did not go far enough.
Republican prosperity
Under Harding and Coolidge, low taxes, laissez-faire policies and protective tariffs supported the 1920s consumer boom in cars, radios and household goods.
Roosevelt's New Deal
From 1933 FDR's alphabet agencies such as the CCC, AAA and TVA provided relief, jobs and reform, transforming the federal government's role.
Wall Street Crash 1929
Panic selling in October 1929 collapsed share prices, ruined speculators who had bought on the margin, and shattered confidence in banks and business.
Battle of Hastings 1066
Decisive battle on 14 October 1066 where William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson, killed by an arrow according to the Bayeux Tapestry.
Domesday Book 1086
Comprehensive land survey ordered by William I recording landholders, livestock and value for taxation across England.
Feudal System
Hierarchical land-holding pyramid: king grants land to barons for knight service; peasants worked land for protection.
Forest Laws
Harsh Norman laws reserving woodlands for royal hunting; punishments included blinding for poaching deer.
Harrying of the North 1069-70
William's brutal campaign destroying villages and crops in Yorkshire and Durham after rebellion; caused mass famine.
Motte and Bailey
Early Norman wooden castle design: raised mound (motte) with keep, enclosed courtyard (bailey) below for garrison.
Balfour Declaration 1917
British letter pledging support for 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine; conflicted with Arab promises.
Camp David Accords 1978
Carter-brokered peace between Sadat's Egypt and Begin's Israel; Egypt recognised Israel, regained Sinai.
Six-Day War 1967
Israeli pre-emptive strike captured Sinai, Golan Heights, West Bank and Gaza from Egypt, Syria and Jordan.
Suez Crisis 1956
British, French and Israeli invasion after Nasser nationalised the canal; US pressure forced humiliating withdrawal.
UN Partition Plan 1947
Resolution 181 dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem internationalised; rejected by Arabs.
Yom Kippur War 1973
Egyptian-Syrian surprise attack on Jewish holy day; led to OPEC oil embargo against Israel's supporters.
Bloody Code 1688-1815
Period when over 200 offences carried death penalty, including theft of goods worth more than 5 shillings.
Derek Bentley 1953
Hanged for murder despite Craig firing the shot; controversial case that fuelled campaign against capital punishment.
Pentonville Prison 1842
Model prison built on separate system: solitary confinement with hard labour to encourage reflection and reform.
Robert Peel 1829
Home Secretary who founded the Metropolitan Police; officers nicknamed 'peelers' or 'bobbies' after him.
Transportation
Punishment of sending convicts to colonies, mainly Australia from 1787; abolished 1868 after 162,000 transported.
Wergild
Anglo-Saxon system of compensation paid to victim's family for crimes; varied by social status of victim.
Act of Supremacy 1534
Law declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England, breaking from papal authority in Rome.
Dissolution of Monasteries
1536-40 closure of 800 religious houses; transferred huge wealth and lands to Crown.
Field of Cloth of Gold 1520
Lavish diplomatic meeting near Calais between Henry VIII and Francis I of France organised by Wolsey.
Pilgrimage of Grace 1536
Major northern rebellion led by Robert Aske against religious changes; 30,000 marched in Yorkshire before being crushed.
Thomas Cromwell
Chief minister 1532-40 who engineered the break with Rome and Dissolution of Monasteries; executed July 1540.
Thomas Wolsey
Cardinal and Lord Chancellor 1515-29; fell from power after failing to secure Henry's divorce from Catherine of Aragon.
Brown v Board of Education 1954
Supreme Court ruling that segregated public schools were unconstitutional, overturning the 'separate but equal' principle.
Civil Rights Act 1964
Landmark law that banned segregation in public places and outlawed discrimination in employment on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
March on Washington 1963
Around 250,000 people marched for civil rights and heard Martin Luther King Jr's 'I Have a Dream' speech, pressing Congress to act.
McCarthyism
Senator Joseph McCarthy's campaign from 1950 of accusing officials of communism, spreading fear until televised hearings discredited him and the Senate censured him in 1954.
Montgomery Bus Boycott 1955-56
Year-long Black boycott of segregated buses after Rosa Parks's arrest, which brought Martin Luther King Jr to prominence and ended bus segregation in Montgomery.
Voting Rights Act 1965
Law that banned literacy tests and allowed federal oversight of voter registration, dramatically increasing Black voter registration in the South.
Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin closed land routes into West Berlin, but a Western airlift supplied the city for almost a year until the blockade was lifted.
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
Discovery of Soviet missile sites on Cuba brought the superpowers close to nuclear war before Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles.
Detente and SALT 1
The easing of tension around 1972, when the SALT 1 agreement signed by Nixon and Brezhnev limited anti-ballistic missile systems and froze missile launcher numbers.
Tehran Conference 1943
First meeting of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill, agreeing that Britain and the USA would open a second front in Western Europe in 1944.
Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan
The 1947 US policy of containment, backed in 1948 by around $13 billion of Marshall Aid to rebuild Western Europe and reduce communism's appeal.
Yalta and Potsdam 1945
Conferences that divided Germany and Berlin into four occupation zones, while disagreements over Poland and reparations deepened distrust.
Alexander Fleming 1928
Scottish bacteriologist who discovered penicillin from accidental mould contamination; mass-produced by Florey and Chain.
Edward Jenner 1796
English doctor who developed smallpox vaccination using cowpox after observing milkmaids' immunity.
Four Humours
Ancient Greek theory by Hippocrates that health depended on balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.
Galen
Roman physician (c.129-216 AD) whose anatomical works dominated medicine for 1500 years despite dissecting animals not humans.
John Snow 1854
Doctor who proved cholera was waterborne by mapping deaths around the Broad Street pump in Soho, London.
Vesalius 1543
Flemish anatomist who published 'On the Fabric of the Human Body', correcting Galen through human dissection.
Enabling Act 1933
Passed after the Reichstag Fire, the Act let Hitler's government make laws without the Reichstag, providing the legal foundation of the dictatorship.
Hyperinflation 1923
After the French occupation of the Ruhr, the government printed money until the mark became worthless, wiping out savings before the Rentenmark restored stability.
Munich Putsch 1923
Hitler's failed armed takeover in Bavaria; his trial publicity and prison time writing Mein Kampf led him to switch to winning power through elections.
Nazi control and terror
The SS and Gestapo, Goebbels's propaganda, and the Night of the Long Knives in 1934 secured Hitler's position as Führer after Hindenburg's death.
Rise to power 1929-33
Depression unemployment of around six million by 1932 fuelled Nazi electoral success, and backstairs intrigue made Hitler Chancellor in January 1933.
Weimar Republic
The democratic republic set up after 1918, with a constitution agreed at Weimar in 1919 featuring proportional representation and Article 48 emergency powers.
Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin's closure of road and rail access to West Berlin; defeated by 11-month Anglo-American airlift.
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
13-day October standoff when USSR placed nuclear missiles in Cuba; Kennedy's quarantine forced Khrushchev to withdraw.
Detente 1970s
Period of relaxed tensions including SALT I (1972), Helsinki Accords (1975) and Apollo-Soyuz docking.
Marshall Plan 1948
US aid programme of $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; Stalin forced satellites to refuse.
Truman Doctrine 1947
US pledge to contain communism by aiding 'free peoples'; sent $400m to Greece and Turkey.
Yalta Conference 1945
February meeting of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill agreeing post-war division of Europe and Soviet entry to UN.

the-origins-course-of-the-first-world-wa.d: The Origins & Course of the First World War 1905-18
terms: Armistice 1918
Ceasefire signed 11 November in Compiegne forest railway carriage; followed German revolution and Kaiser's abdication.
Assassination at Sarajevo 1914
Gavrilo Princip's killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June triggered Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia.
Battle of Verdun 1916
10-month French defence against German attack; symbol of French resistance, around 700,000 total casualties.
Battle of the Somme 1916
British offensive 1 July - 18 November; 60,000 casualties on first day, around 1 million total casualties.
Schlieffen Plan
German strategy to defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning east on Russia; failed at Marne.
Trench Warfare
Static system of opposing trenches across Western Front; 'no man's land' between, dominated by machine guns and artillery.
April Theses 1917
Lenin's programme on return from Switzerland: 'peace, land, bread' and 'all power to the Soviets'.
Bloody Sunday 1905
Tsarist troops fired on Father Gapon's petition march to Winter Palace; around 200 killed, sparked 1905 Revolution.
Collectivisation 1928-40
Stalin's forced merging of farms into kolkhozy; eliminated kulaks, caused 1932-33 Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) killing 5-7 million.
Doctors' Plot 1953
Antisemitic conspiracy alleging Jewish doctors planned to murder Soviet leaders; ended by Stalin's death in March.
Great Terror 1936-38
Stalin's purges: show trials of Bukharin, Zinoviev, Kamenev; 750,000 executions; gulag population reached 1.6 million.
Kronstadt Mutiny 1921
Naval base sailors' revolt against Bolshevik rule; brutally crushed by Trotsky, prompted NEP.
Dien Bien Phu 1954
Decisive Viet Minh victory over French forces under Giap; ended French Indochina, led to Geneva Accords.
Fall of Saigon 1975
30 April capture by North Vietnamese; helicopter evacuations from US embassy ended American involvement.
Geneva Accords 1954
Agreement partitioning Vietnam at 17th parallel pending elections; US blocked elections to prevent Ho Chi Minh victory.
Gulf of Tonkin 1964
Alleged North Vietnamese attack on USS Maddox; resolution gave Johnson power for full military involvement.
My Lai Massacre 1968
US troops under Lt. Calley killed 504 unarmed civilians; cover-up exposed 1969, devastated US moral authority.
Tet Offensive 1968
Viet Cong surprise attacks on 100 cities during lunar new year; military defeat but US public confidence collapsed.

medicine-in-britain-c1250-present-britis.d: Medicine in Britain c1250-Present & British Sector of the Western Front
terms: Beveridge Report 1942
Identified five 'Giant Evils' (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness); blueprint for post-war welfare state.
General Strike 1926
Nine-day TUC strike supporting miners against wage cuts; defeated by Baldwin government, weakened union power.
Good Friday Agreement 1998
Peace deal ending Troubles in Northern Ireland; devolved Assembly, decommissioning of paramilitary weapons.
Liberal Reforms 1906-11
Welfare measures: school meals (1906), old age pensions (1908), National Insurance (1911) under Asquith and Lloyd George.
Suffragettes
Militant women's suffrage movement led by Emmeline Pankhurst from 1903; hunger strikes, Cat and Mouse Act 1913.
Thatcher 1979-90
First female PM; privatised industries, defeated 1984-85 miners' strike, Falklands War 1982.
Civil War 1918-21
The Reds defended the revolution against the Whites and foreign intervention; Trotsky's Red Army and control of the centre secured Bolshevik victory.
Collectivisation
From 1928 Stalin merged peasant farms into collective farms (kolkhozy) to control grain; 'kulaks' were deported and famine struck in 1932-33.
February Revolution 1917
Strikes and bread queues in Petrograd, joined by mutinying soldiers, forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate in March 1917.
New Economic Policy 1921
Lenin's retreat from War Communism, allowing peasants to sell surplus grain and small businesses to trade, after famine and the Kronstadt rising.
October Revolution 1917
The Bolsheviks, organised by Trotsky and led by Lenin, seized key points in Petrograd and overthrew the Provisional Government.
The Great Terror
Stalin's purges of the 1930s: show trials of Old Bolsheviks, mass NKVD arrests, the Gulag camps, and the decimation of the Red Army officer corps.
Berlin Blockade 1948-49
Stalin's closure of road and rail access to West Berlin; defeated by 11-month Anglo-American airlift.
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
13-day October standoff when USSR placed nuclear missiles in Cuba; Kennedy's quarantine forced Khrushchev to withdraw.
Detente 1970s
Period of relaxed tensions including SALT I (1972), Helsinki Accords (1975) and Apollo-Soyuz docking.
Marshall Plan 1948
US aid programme of $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; Stalin forced satellites to refuse.
Truman Doctrine 1947
US pledge to contain communism by aiding 'free peoples'; sent $400m to Greece and Turkey.
Yalta Conference 1945
February meeting of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill agreeing post-war division of Europe and Soviet entry to UN.
Beveridge Report 1942
Identified five 'Giant Evils' (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness); blueprint for post-war welfare state.
General Strike 1926
Nine-day TUC strike supporting miners against wage cuts; defeated by Baldwin government, weakened union power.
Good Friday Agreement 1998
Peace deal ending Troubles in Northern Ireland; devolved Assembly, decommissioning of paramilitary weapons.
Liberal Reforms 1906-11
Welfare measures: school meals (1906), old age pensions (1908), National Insurance (1911) under Asquith and Lloyd George.
Suffragettes
Militant women's suffrage movement led by Emmeline Pankhurst from 1903; hunger strikes, Cat and Mouse Act 1913.
Thatcher 1979-90
First female PM; privatised industries, defeated 1984-85 miners' strike, Falklands War 1982.
Catholics and recusancy
Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services faced heavy fines after 1581, while missionary priests such as Edmund Campion were executed as traitors.
Elizabeth I's government
Elizabeth ruled through her court, a Privy Council guided by ministers such as William Cecil (Lord Burghley), and occasional Parliaments.
Mary, Queen of Scots
The Catholic claimant held captive in England; evidence of her involvement in the Babington Plot led to her execution at Fotheringhay in 1587.
Poverty and the Poor Laws
Rising population and the terrible harvests of the 1590s increased vagrancy, and the 1601 Poor Law made each parish responsible for its own poor.
Spanish Armada 1588
Philip II's invasion fleet was scattered by English fireships at Calais and shattered by storms as it fled around Scotland and Ireland.
The 'Golden Age'
A flourishing of drama, music and exploration, with playhouses such as the Globe (1599) and voyagers like Drake, although life stayed harsh for most people.
Crises of the 1950s-60s
Confrontations such as Hungary 1956, the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought repeated danger of war.
Detente and its collapse
Arms control agreements like SALT 1 and the Helsinki Accords eased tension until the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 triggered a 'Second Cold War'.
End of the Cold War
Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika, the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe and the fall of the Berlin Wall preceded the dissolution of the USSR in 1991.
Grand Alliance 1941-45
The wartime partnership of the USA, USSR and Britain against the Axis, strained at Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam by disputes over Eastern Europe.
Origins of the Cold War
Between 1945 and 1949 the Iron Curtain, Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin Blockade and creation of NATO divided Europe into rival blocs.
Post-Cold War world
After 1991 the USA stood as sole superpower; the 9/11 attacks of 2001 led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, while Russia grew more assertive by 2010.
Consolidation of power 1933-34
The Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, banning of parties and the Night of the Long Knives made Hitler Führer of a one-party state by 1934.
Persecution of the Jews
Persecution escalated from the 1933 boycott through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and Kristallnacht in 1938 to ghettos and the Holocaust during the war.
Propaganda
Goebbels's ministry controlled newspapers, cheap 'people's receiver' radios, film and mass rallies such as Nuremberg to spread the Hitler myth.
The police state
The SS and Gestapo, helped by informers and concentration camps, crushed opposition, while courts and judges were brought under Nazi control.
Wartime life and resistance
War brought rationing, bombing and total mobilisation, and resistance grew from groups like the White Rose to the July 1944 bomb plot.
Youth and education
The Hitler Youth and League of German Maidens trained boys for war and girls for motherhood, while school subjects were rewritten around race and loyalty.

migration-to-britain-c1000-to-c2010.d: Migration to Britain c1000 to c2010
terms: Empire Windrush 1948
Ship arriving at Tilbury on 22 June 1948 carrying 492 Caribbean migrants; symbol of post-war Commonwealth migration.
Huguenots 1685
French Protestants fleeing Louis XIV's revocation of Edict of Nantes; brought silk weaving skills to Spitalfields.
Irish Migration 1840s
Famine refugees fleeing potato blight; over 500,000 settled in Liverpool, Manchester and Glasgow by 1851.
Jewish Migration 1880-1914
Around 150,000 Eastern European Jews fled Russian pogroms; settled in East End of London.
Notting Hill Riots 1958
Racial violence in west London where white youths attacked Caribbean residents over three nights in August/September.
Race Relations Act 1965
First UK law banning racial discrimination in public places under Harold Wilson's Labour government.
Causes of the Civil War
Disputes over religion, including Laud's reforms and the Scottish Prayer Book rebellion, plus money and royal power, led to war between king and Parliament in 1642.
Cromwell and the Interregnum
Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 to 1658, campaigning in Ireland and Scotland and briefly imposing the Rule of the Major-Generals.
First Civil War 1642-46
Royalists fought Parliamentarians across England; Parliament's New Model Army won the decisive victory at Naseby in 1645.
Personal Rule 1629-40
Charles I governed for eleven years without calling Parliament, raising money through devices such as Ship Money and fines.
Regicide 1649
Charles I was tried for treason and beheaded in January 1649; the monarchy and House of Lords were abolished and England became a republic.
Restoration 1660
Charles II was invited back as king in 1660; his reign included the Plague of 1665, the Great Fire of 1666 and the Exclusion Crisis before his death in 1685.

power-monarchy-democracy-in-britain-c100.d: Power: Monarchy & Democracy in Britain c1000 to 2014
terms: Bill of Rights 1689
Constitutional law after Glorious Revolution limiting monarchy and establishing parliamentary sovereignty.
Chartists 1838-48
Working class movement demanding six points including universal male suffrage and secret ballot; three petitions failed.
English Civil War 1642-51
War between Charles I (Royalists) and Parliament (Roundheads); ended with Charles's execution in January 1649.
Magna Carta 1215
Charter limiting King John's power; clause 39 established no free man should be imprisoned except by lawful judgment.
Peterloo Massacre 1819
Cavalry charge into crowd of 60,000 demanding parliamentary reform at St Peter's Field, Manchester; 18 killed.
Simon de Montfort 1265
Baron who summoned first parliament including commoners (knights and burgesses) after defeating Henry III at Lewes.
Battle of Hastings 1066
Decisive battle on 14 October 1066 where William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson, killed by an arrow according to the Bayeux Tapestry.
Domesday Book 1086
Comprehensive land survey ordered by William I recording landholders, livestock and value for taxation across England.
Feudal System
Hierarchical land-holding pyramid: king grants land to barons for knight service; peasants worked land for protection.
Forest Laws
Harsh Norman laws reserving woodlands for royal hunting; punishments included blinding for poaching deer.
Harrying of the North 1069-70
William's brutal campaign destroying villages and crops in Yorkshire and Durham after rebellion; caused mass famine.
Motte and Bailey
Early Norman wooden castle design: raised mound (motte) with keep, enclosed courtyard (bailey) below for garrison.

the-peoples-health-c1250-to-present.d: The People's Health c1250 to Present
terms: Black Death 1348-49
Plague killed around a third or more of England's population; responses included prayer, flight, quarantine attempts and blaming bad air.
Great Plague 1665
During London's last major plague outbreak, infected households were shut up and marked with red crosses, searchers counted the dead, and victims were buried in plague pits.
Industrial cities and cholera
Rapid urban growth created slums with foul water, and cholera epidemics repeatedly struck Britain from 1831-32 onwards.
Medieval towns c1250-1500
Overcrowded streets, shared wells, cesspits and butchers' waste threatened health; town authorities issued sanitation rules but enforcement was weak.
Public health reform
Chadwick's 1842 report, John Snow's 1854 Broad Street pump study, Bazalgette's sewers and the Public Health Acts of 1848 and 1875 transformed towns.
Twentieth-century welfare
The Liberal reforms of 1906-11, council housing and the creation of the NHS in 1948 made government responsible for the people's health.
Cnut's North Sea Empire
The Danish conquest of England made Cnut king in 1016, and he ruled England, Denmark and Norway together until his death in 1035.
Longships
Fast, shallow-draught vessels powered by sail and oars that could cross open seas yet row far up rivers, making surprise raids and long voyages possible.
North Atlantic settlement
Norse settlers colonised Iceland from around 870 and Greenland under Erik the Red from around 985, and briefly reached Vinland in North America around 1000.
Raid on Lindisfarne 793
The Viking attack on the Northumbrian monastery shocked Christian Europe and traditionally marks the start of the Viking Age.
The Danelaw
The area of northern and eastern England under Danish law and settlement after the Great Army's campaigns, with Jorvik (York) as a major centre.
Trade and towns
Viking networks stretched from Dublin and Hedeby to the rivers of Russia, exchanging furs, slaves and silver, and building thriving trading towns.
